content: 1. The coadministration of enasidenib and ethinylestradiol may alter the concentrations of combined hormonal contraceptives, either increasing or decreasing their levels. The clinical significance of this interaction remains unknown. Close monitoring is advised. 2. Encorafenib, a BCRP inhibitor, may increase the concentration and toxicity of BCRP substrates, including ethinylestradiol. Therapy modification or close monitoring is recommended. 3. Encorafenib may decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative drugs or nonhormonal contraceptives should be used, as coadministration may reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Women of childbearing potential should use highly effective nonhormonal contraception during treatment and for two weeks after the last dose of encorafenib. 4. Ethinylestradiol may reduce the effects of enoxaparin through pharmacodynamic antagonism, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disorders. This combination is contraindicated. 5. Enzalutamide decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative drugs or nonhormonal contraceptives are recommended. 6. Ethinylestradiol may increase the levels or effects of eplerenone by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, and close monitoring is advised. 7. Erythromycin base may decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are advised. 8. Antibiotics, including erythromycin ethylsuccinate, lactobionate, and stearate, may decrease the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 9. Eslcarbazepine acetate decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative drugs or additional nonhormonal birth control methods are recommended. 10. Etravirine decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced, and nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 11. Ethinylestradiol reduces the effects of exemestane through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Exemestane should not be coadministered with estrogens or estrogen-containing products. 12. Ethinylestradiol may decrease the hypoglycemic effects of antidiabetics, such as exenatide, by impairing glucose tolerance. Patients should take oral contraceptives at least one hour before exenatide administration. Close monitoring is advised. 13. Fedratinib increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Coadministration with dual CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 inhibitors should be avoided. 14. Felbamate decreases the levels of ethinylestradiol through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 15. Fexinidazole increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP2E1 metabolism. Coadministration is not recommended due to the risk of adverse effects. 16. Fezolinetant levels and peak plasma concentrations are increased when coadministered with CYP1A2 inhibitors. This combination is contraindicated. 17. Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of finerenone by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Serum potassium should be monitored during therapy initiation and dosage adjustments. 18. Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of flibanserin by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Adverse effects may occur if coadministered with multiple weak CYP3A4 inhibitors. 19. Fluconazole increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Close monitoring is recommended. 20. Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of fluvoxamine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 21. Fosamprenavir may alter hormone levels and decrease amprenavir AUC, potentially leading to loss of virologic response. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 22. Fostemsavir increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Ethinylestradiol doses should not exceed 30 mcg/day. 23. Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of frovatriptan by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 24. Grapefruit increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 25. Ethinylestradiol increases green tea levels by decreasing elimination. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 26. Griseofulvin decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 27. Ethinylestradiol reduces the effects of hemin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 28. Ethinylestradiol reduces the effects of heparin through pharmacodynamic antagonism, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disorders. This combination is contraindicated. 29. Estrogens in high systemic doses may render tissues partially resistant to hyaluronidase. Larger amounts of hyaluronidase may be required for equivalent dispersing effects. 30. Idelalisib increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Coadministration with sensitive CYP3A4 substrates should be avoided. 31. Iloperidone increases the levels of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 32. Ethinylestradiol may increase antidepressant serum concentrations by decreasing oxidative metabolism of TCAs. Potential for increased TCA adverse effects exists. 33. Indinavir may cause significant changes in estrogen plasma levels, reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 34. Ethinylestradiol decreases the effects of insulin and other antidiabetics by impairing glucose tolerance. Glycemic control should be monitored in diabetic patients. 35. Isavuconazonium sulfate increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Coadministration is not recommended. 36. Istradefylline increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose reduction of sensitive CYP3A4 substrates should be considered. 37. Itraconazole increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 38. Ivosidenib decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Coadministration with sensitive CYP3A4 substrates should be avoided. 39. Ketoconazole increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 40. Ethinylestradiol decreases lamotrigine levels by inducing hepatic clearance. Plasma concentrations of lamotrigine may be significantly reduced, requiring close monitoring. 41. Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of lapatinib by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 42. Larotrectinib increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 43. Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of lemborexant by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification or close monitoring is recommended.
